questions.q: A transition element is defined as one that has:
questions.solution:
A transition element has a **partly filled d subshell**, either in the atom or in a common ion.

This is why zinc, cadmium and mercury ($d^{10}s^{2}$, and $d^{10}$ in their only common oxidation state) are **not** counted as true transition metals — and why they are colourless and poorly catalytic.
options: a partially filled d subshell in its ground state or in a common oxidation state

questions.q: Transition metal ions are usually coloured because of:
questions.solution:
In a ligand field the five d orbitals split, and an electron can absorb visible light to jump between them — a **d–d transition**. The colour seen is the complement of what is absorbed.

Ions with $d^{0}$ or $d^{10}$ configurations ($\text{Sc}^{3+}$, $\text{Zn}^{2+}$) have no such jump available and are **colourless**.

Across the lanthanoids, electrons enter the inner **4f** orbitals, which shield the nuclear charge very poorly. The effective nuclear charge therefore grows and the radius **steadily shrinks**.

**The consequence that matters:** Zr and Hf, and Nb and Ta, end up almost identical in size and are notoriously hard to separate. It also makes the third-row transition metals unexpectedly dense.
options: increase in size across the lanthanoid series
steady decrease in size across the lanthanoid series

questions.q: The highest oxidation state shown by manganese is:
questions.solution:
Manganese is $3d^{5}4s^{2}$ — seven electrons available, so the maximum is $\mathbf{+7}$, as in $\text{KMnO}_{4}$.

Variable oxidation states are a hallmark of the d block, because the $3d$ and $4s$ energies are so close that electrons can be removed from either.

questions.q: Transition metals are good catalysts mainly because they:
questions.solution:
Two reasons, both structural: **variable oxidation states** let the metal accept and donate electrons in intermediate steps, and their surfaces **adsorb** reactants, holding them close and weakening their bonds.

Iron in the Haber process and vanadium pentoxide in the Contact process both work this way.
options: show variable oxidation states and provide a surface for adsorption

questions.q: Find the number of unpaired electrons in the $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ion. (Atomic number of Fe $= 26$.)
questions.solution:
Fe is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{6}4s^{2}$. Losing three electrons — $4s$ first, then one $3d$ — gives $\text{Fe}^{3+} = [\text{Ar}]3d^{5}$.

Five d electrons occupy five orbitals singly (Hund's rule), so there are $\mathbf{5}$ unpaired electrons.

A half-filled $d^{5}$ shell is unusually stable, which is why $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is more stable than $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in aqueous solution.

questions.q: Find the spin-only magnetic moment (in Bohr magnetons) for an ion with $2$ unpaired electrons, correct to two decimal places. Use $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$.
questions.solution:
$\mu = \sqrt{2 \times 4} = \sqrt{8} = \mathbf{2.83}$ BM.

The measured moment is how the number of unpaired electrons is found experimentally — and hence the oxidation state and geometry.

questions.q: Find the oxidation state of manganese in $\text{KMnO}_{4}$.
questions.solution:
$\text{K}$ is $+1$ and each $\text{O}$ is $-2$.

$1 + x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = \mathbf{+7}$ — the highest manganese reaches, which is why permanganate is such a strong oxidising agent.

questions.q: Find the oxidation state of chromium in the dichromate ion $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$.
Find the number of unpaired electrons in $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. (Atomic number of Cu $= 29$.)
questions.solution:
Cu is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{1}$ (the anomalous configuration — a full d shell is worth the promotion).

$\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{9}$, so one orbital holds a single electron: $\mathbf{1}$ unpaired.

That single electron is why copper(II) salts are blue and copper(I) salts are colourless ($d^{10}$).

questions.q: Explain why transition metals have high melting points, show variable oxidation states, and form coloured compounds.
questions.solution:
**High melting points.** Both the $ns$ and the $(n-1)d$ electrons take part in metallic bonding, so the bonds are strong and numerous. The more unpaired d electrons, the stronger the bonding — which is why the melting points peak in the middle of each series (tungsten, at $3683$ K, is the highest of any metal).

Zinc, cadmium and mercury, with no unpaired d electrons, are the exceptions: mercury is liquid at room temperature.

**Variable oxidation states.** The $3d$ and $4s$ energies are very close, so electrons can be removed from either shell with little difference in cost. The states differ by one unit, unlike the p block where they differ by two.

**Coloured compounds.** In a complex the d orbitals split by an energy corresponding to visible light. An electron absorbs a photon and jumps the gap; the transmitted light is the complement of what was absorbed.

The size of the gap depends on the ligand, which is why the same metal gives different colours with different ligands — $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_{2}\text{O})_{4}]^{2+}$ is pale blue while $[\text{Cu}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}]^{2+}$ is deep blue.

questions.q: What is lanthanoid contraction? State its cause and two of its consequences.
questions.solution:
**What it is.** A steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii from La to Lu across the lanthanoid series, in spite of the growing number of electrons.

**Cause.** The added electrons go into **4f** orbitals, which are diffuse and shield the nucleus very poorly. Each step adds a proton whose pull is barely offset, so the effective nuclear charge rises and every shell is drawn in.

**Consequences.**

1. **Second and third transition series resemble each other closely.** Zr ($160$ pm) and Hf ($159$ pm) are almost the same size and chemically near-identical, and separating them is one of the harder problems in inorganic chemistry. The same holds for Nb/Ta and Mo/W.

2. **Basicity of the hydroxides falls** from $\text{La}(\text{OH})_{3}$ to $\text{Lu}(\text{OH})_{3}$, as the smaller, more charge-dense ions hold the hydroxide more tightly.

3. The small, regular size difference is what makes **ion-exchange separation** of the individual lanthanoids possible at all.

questions.q: Describe the preparation of potassium permanganate from pyrolusite, and write its reaction with acidified ferrous sulphate.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — fusion.** Pyrolusite ($\text{MnO}_{2}$) is fused with $\text{KOH}$ in the presence of air or an oxidising agent such as $\text{KNO}_{3}$, giving green potassium manganate:

$2\text{MnO}_{2} + 4\text{KOH} + \text{O}_{2} \to 2\text{K}_{2}\text{MnO}_{4} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Step 2 — oxidation.** The manganate(VI) is oxidised to permanganate(VII), electrolytically or with chlorine or ozone:

$3\text{MnO}_{4}^{2-} + 4\text{H}^{+} \to 2\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} + \text{MnO}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

(a disproportionation: manganese goes both up to $+7$ and down to $+4$). The purple solution is crystallised out.

**With acidified ferrous sulphate.** In acid, permanganate is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ and takes five electrons:

$\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 8\text{H}^{+} + 5e^{-} \to \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

$\text{Fe}^{2+} \to \text{Fe}^{3+} + e^{-}$

**Overall:**

$\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 5\text{Fe}^{2+} + 8\text{H}^{+} \to \text{Mn}^{2+} + 5\text{Fe}^{3+} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

The purple colour vanishes as $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ forms, which is why permanganate is a **self-indicating** titrant — the first drop of excess turns the flask pink.

questions.q: Give three ways in which the actinoids differ from the lanthanoids.
questions.solution:
1. **Range of oxidation states.** Lanthanoids are overwhelmingly $+3$; actinoids show $+3$ to $+7$ (uranium reaches $+6$, neptunium $+7$), because the $5f$, $6d$ and $7s$ energies are much closer together than the corresponding lanthanoid levels.

2. **Radioactivity.** All actinoids are radioactive, and those beyond uranium do not occur in nature at all; the lanthanoids (bar promethium) are stable.

3. **Greater tendency to complex formation,** because the actinoid ions are larger and more highly charged.

4. **Actinoid contraction is sharper** than the lanthanoid contraction, since $5f$ electrons shield even more poorly than $4f$.

5. Their chemistry is far harder to study — the elements are scarce, intensely radioactive and often available only in microgram quantities.

questions.q: What are interstitial compounds? Why are transition metals so good at forming them, and how does this change their properties?
questions.solution:
**What they are.** Compounds in which small atoms — H, C, N, B — occupy the **gaps (interstices)** in the metal's crystal lattice, without changing its basic structure.

They are usually **non-stoichiometric**, with formulae such as $\text{TiC}$, $\text{Fe}_{3}\text{H}$, $\text{VH}_{0.56}$ — a sign that they are not ordinary valence compounds.

**Why transition metals.** Their lattices have interstices of just the right size, and their metallic bonding is unaffected by a guest atom slipping in.

**Changed properties.**

1. **Much harder** — the trapped atoms block the planes from sliding over one another. Steel is iron with carbon in the interstices, and tungsten carbide cuts steel.

2. **Higher melting point** than the pure metal.

3. **Metallic conductivity is retained**, unlike in a salt.

4. **Chemically inert.**

Interstitial hydrides are also the reason some transition metals catalyse hydrogenation: the hydrogen is taken into the surface and its bond weakened before it ever meets the substrate.
